Opinion

The CFO's Job in a Boom Is to Say No to Cheap Stories

Record IPOs, record bond issuance for AI and a market that rewards ambition. This is exactly when finance directors earn their salary: by asking the boring questions nobody wants to hear.

Opinion. The views expressed are the author's own.

Mohamed Ramadan
26 October 2026 · 3 min readLeadershipAIIPOs & Deals

Key points

  • In a boom, capital is cheap and stories are expensive: the risk is paying for narratives rather than cash flows.
  • The CFO's value is to translate enthusiasm into assumptions that can be tested.
  • Saying no is easier when the organisation has agreed in advance what it will not do.

Every boom has a story, and every story has a spreadsheet that makes it look inevitable. In 2026, the story is artificial intelligence, and the numbers are extraordinary. The five largest American hyperscalers issued about $230bn of corporate bonds in the first nine months of the year, according to research from the Bank of Korea. IPO proceeds have reached record levels. Boards everywhere are asked the same question: what is our AI strategy, and why are we not spending more on it?

I have sat in the finance director's chair. I know how this moment feels from the inside. The pressure to say yes is enormous, and it rarely looks like pressure. It looks like optimism, momentum and fear of missing out.

Cheap capital, expensive stories

In a boom, money is easy to raise. That is precisely what makes it dangerous. When investors are eager, the cost of capital seems low, and projects that would never pass a disciplined review suddenly look reasonable. The danger is not that the technology is false. The danger is that the price paid for it assumes a future that is far from certain.

The CFO's first duty is to separate the story from the cash flows. What revenue will this investment generate, when, and under what assumptions? What happens if adoption is slower, prices fall faster or the assets become obsolete in three years instead of seven? Those questions are not hostile to innovation. They are the conditions for financing it sustainably.

In a boom, the most valuable word in the finance function is not yes or no. It is "assuming".

The mismatch nobody likes to discuss

One risk deserves particular attention: the mismatch between long-dated financing and short-lived assets. Chips and servers can lose much of their value within a few years, while the bonds that financed them run for a decade or more. If the economics of the assets change, the debt remains. This is a classic treasury problem, and it does not disappear because the technology is new.

Decide in advance what you will not do

The hardest part of saying no is doing it in the moment. The best protection is to agree the rules before the pressure arrives: the maximum leverage the company will accept, the payback period for new investments, the share of capital that can go to a single theme. When those limits are written down and approved by the board, the CFO is not fighting the CEO's ambition. They are defending a decision the company already made.

It also helps to change the language. Instead of rejecting a project, the finance team can ask for a staged plan: a first phase with clear milestones, funded modestly, followed by larger commitments only when the evidence arrives. This protects the downside without killing the opportunity.

Humility as a financial discipline

Behind all this sits a personal quality I value more than any technical skill: humility. Nobody knows how the AI cycle will end. The most dangerous executives are those who are certain, in either direction. The best finance teams hold two ideas at once: this technology is transformative, and many of the investments made in its name will fail.

The bottom line

Booms are not won by those who spend the most, but by those who are still standing when the cycle turns. The CFO's job is to make sure the company is one of them. Sometimes that means saying no to a very good story.

Sources

  • Herald Business, reporting Bank of Korea research on hyperscaler bond issuance, 2026
  • Mohamed Ramadan, "Borrowing for Intelligence" and "The IPO Record", October 2026

Central Banks Should Stop Apologising for Fighting Inflation

The Bank of England is preparing to raise rates into an energy shock. It will be accused of hurting households. The real harm would come from letting inflation settle in.

Opinion. The views expressed are the author's own.

Mohamed Ramadan
25 October 2026 · 3 min readUKDebt & Rates

Key points

  • UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September; three of nine MPC members already voted for a hike.
  • Raising rates into a supply shock is uncomfortable, but expectations, once lost, are costly to rebuild.
  • Central banks should explain more and apologise less: credibility is the cheapest tool they have.

In November, the Bank of England is expected to raise Bank Rate from 3.75% to 4%. On 28 October, market pricing implied a probability of around 97%. The criticism has already started: why tighten when the inflation comes from energy prices, when growth is weak and households are still recovering from the last squeeze?

The question is fair. My answer is that the Bank should go ahead, and that it should stop sounding apologetic about it.

A supply shock is not a free pass

Textbook economics says central banks should "look through" supply shocks. If prices rise because energy is scarce, higher interest rates will not produce more oil or gas. They will only slow the rest of the economy.

That advice is correct for a one-off shock that leaves expectations unchanged. It is dangerous when inflation is already above target and has been for years. UK inflation rose to 3.5% in September, from 3.1% in August. When households and companies have lived through repeated price surges, they begin to expect them. Wages, contracts and prices start to build in higher inflation. At that point, the shock is no longer temporary.

The cost of acting early is a few months of slower growth. The cost of acting late is years of credibility lost.

The lesson of the last decade

Central banks learned this lesson painfully in 2021 and 2022. They described inflation as transitory, waited too long and then had to raise rates faster and further than anyone expected. The adjustment was brutal for borrowers. It would have been gentler if it had started earlier.

The split on the Monetary Policy Committee, with three of nine members already voting for a hike in September, shows that the Bank is aware of the risk. A move now is a smaller, more predictable step than a larger one later.

Explain more, apologise less

What the Bank should avoid is the tone of an institution ashamed of its own mandate. Price stability is not a technocratic obsession. Inflation hits hardest those with the least protection: people on fixed incomes, renters, savers with cash, workers without bargaining power. A central bank that defends price stability is defending them.

That message needs to be told clearly and often. Credibility is the cheapest tool a central bank has. When markets and households believe the Bank will do what is necessary, it usually has to do less.

The fiscal side of the bargain

Monetary policy does not act alone. A Budget that adds support for households while the Bank is trying to cool demand makes the Bank's job harder. Coordination does not mean the Treasury takes orders from Threadneedle Street. It means both sides acknowledge that they are pulling on the same economy.

The bottom line

A rate rise into an energy shock will be unpopular. Letting inflation settle in would be worse. The Bank of England should act, explain why and resist the temptation to apologise for doing its job.

Sources

  • Office for National Statistics, September 2026 CPI, as reported by HomeOwners Alliance
  • Cambridge Currencies, Bank of England September 2026 decision
  • RateProbability and BlueGamma, market-implied probabilities, 27–28 October 2026

The Price of Time: Britain's 6% Gilt Has Just Ended the Era of Free Slow Money

A 6% gilt marks the end of an era in which slow, opaque money was free. The winners of the next decade will be those who make time cheap again.

Mohamed Ramadan
15 October 2026 · 7 min readUKDebt & RatesAfrica

Key points

  • On 1 October 2026, the yield on Britain's 30-year gilt touched 6.03%, a level last seen in January 1998.
  • Every 0.25 point on gilt yields adds roughly £2.5 billion a year to UK debt interest.
  • £1 million stuck for three days now costs about £308 in lost interest, against £8 in 2021.
  • Sending $200 to sub-Saharan Africa costs 8.46% on average, against 6.36% worldwide.

On the morning of 1 October 2026, the yield on Britain’s 30-year government bond touched 6.03%. The last time London paid that much to borrow for a generation was January 1998, a year after the Bank of England was handed the keys to interest rates and a year before the euro was born.

Most commentary will treat this as a British story: a new Chancellor, a Budget on 28 October, a nervous bond market. I want to argue something different, and more uncomfortable.

My thesis is simple: a 6% gilt marks the end of an era in which slow, opaque money was free. For fifteen years, near-zero rates hid the true cost of the way money moves between Britain and Africa. That subsidy is gone. Every day a payment waits, every pound that sits idle, every point of spread on a transfer is now a measurable loss, and Africa pays the largest share of it. The winners of the next decade will not be those with the cleverest token, but those who make time cheap again.

Here is the case.

1. The staircase, not the spike

Markets like to call every bad day a “spike”. But look at the sequence. The 30-year gilt went above 5% during the 2022 mini-budget crisis, then to 5.69% in September 2025, to 5.78% in May 2026, to about 5.9% in September, and to 6.03% on 1 October. The 10-year reached 5.51%, its highest since July 2007.

When a spike repeats itself four times in four years, it is not a spike. It is a staircase, and staircases are built on foundations:

  • Energy and war. With the Strait of Hormuz still disrupted and oil back above $100 a barrel, UK inflation has turned up again: 3.1% in August, with the Bank of England itself projecting about 3.75% by year-end and slightly above 4% in early 2027.
  • Washington moved first. The Federal Reserve raised rates to 3.75–4% on 16 September, its first hike since 2023, and most of its policymakers expect more.
  • London’s own arithmetic. The Bank held at 3.75%, but three of its nine policymakers already voted to raise. The Treasury must still sell about £246 billion of gilts this fiscal year.

The point is not that rates are high. It is that nobody serious expects them to return to zero. The Fed’s own projections push the first cuts out to 2028. That changes the economics of everything that is slow.

2. When the bond market writes the Budget, it writes everyone’s budget

In 1993, James Carville, Bill Clinton’s strategist, said that if he were reincarnated he would want to come back as the bond market, because “you can intimidate everybody”. African finance ministers have lived with that intimidation for decades, sitting in London roadshows being told that their spreads reflect their “credibility”.

This autumn, the lecture is being delivered to a G7 Treasury. In March, the Office for Budget Responsibility gave the Chancellor about £23.6 billion of headroom against the fiscal rules. Higher yields have since cut it to an estimated £8.5–16 billion. Every 0.25 point on gilt yields adds roughly £2.5 billion a year to debt interest.

Why should an importer in Douala or a treasurer in Lagos care? Because the gilt and the Treasury bill are the benchmarks against which their own money is priced. Sub-Saharan sovereigns raised about $9.3 billion in Eurobonds between January and September 2026, more than in all of 2025, and their repayments rise from about $3.5 billion in 2026 to $8.6 billion in 2028, according to the World Bank. When the base rate of the world rises, Africa’s bill rises with it, even if nothing in Africa has changed.

3. The hierarchy is blurring at the top, not at the bottom

Here is a comparison nobody in the City will put on a slide. In February 2026, Côte d’Ivoire raised $1.3 billion over 15 years, nearly five times oversubscribed, at an effective 5.39% after hedging into euros. On 1 October, Britain paid 5.51% for 10 years and 6.03% for 30 years in its own currency.

The comparison is imperfect: currencies, maturities and dates differ, and the chart says so. But the order of magnitude makes the argument. The old hierarchy, in which the North borrows cheaply and the South pays for its sins, is blurring at the top. It is not blurring at the bottom: DR Congo’s debut 10-year bond cost 9.5%, and Kenya refinanced at 10.4% a bond originally issued at 6.9%.

This matters for my thesis. If even London now pays for time, then the price of time is no longer a “risk premium” that Africa alone carries. It is a global cost of capital, and the question becomes: who wastes it, and who saves it?

4. The hidden tax: what slow payments really cost

This is where the argument becomes concrete.

Benjamin Franklin wrote in 1748 that “time is money”. For most of the past fifteen years, it wasn’t. With Bank Rate at 0.10% in 2021, £1 million stuck for three days in a correspondent banking chain cost about £8 in lost interest. Nobody noticed, so nobody fixed it.

At today’s 3.75%, the same three days cost about £308. At the 10-year gilt rate, about £453. Same delay, 37 times more expensive.

Now multiply. Every supplier invoice paid from Africa via London. Every payroll. Every FX conversion done on an “indicative” rate that moves before the money lands. Every balance left idle in a non-interest account “just in case”. In a zero-rate world, these were inconveniences. In a 6% world, they are a hidden tax, and the slowest rail pays it.

5. Africa pays the highest toll to receive its own money

The World Bank’s latest data are unambiguous. Sending $200 to sub-Saharan Africa costs 8.46% on average, against 6.36% worldwide, 4.59% through digital channels and 14.99% through a bank. The UN target is 3% by 2030.

High rates make this worse, not better. When money is expensive, every intermediary in the chain has an incentive to hold funds a little longer and to price risk a little higher. Africa does not only pay more to borrow. It pays more to receive.

6. Objections, and why they don’t hold

“Rates will fall again, so this will pass.” Perhaps, eventually. But the Fed does not expect cuts before 2028, and the Bank of England projects inflation above 4% in early 2027. More importantly, a business model that only works at zero rates is not a business model. It is a bet.

“Stablecoins will fix it.” They will help, and London is serious about them. In June 2026, the Bank of England finalised its regime for systemic sterling stablecoins: up to 70% of reserves in UK government debt maturing within six months, the rest at the Bank, and a cap of £40 billion per coin. The FCA regime enters into force on 25 October 2027.

But read the design carefully. A coin at the cap could hold £28 billion of short-dated gilts. London has created a new buyer for its own debt, at the short end, while the pain sits at thirty years. The regime is built first to make sterling tokens safe and to fund the state, not to solve the last mile into Douala, Accra or Lagos. A token settles in minutes. Converting it into CFA francs or naira at a fair rate, with compliance, liquidity and a bank account at the other end, still does not. The bottleneck is not the technology. It is liquidity, trust and the last mile.

“This is a British problem.” Section 2 answers it: the benchmark channel carries London’s price of time straight into every African balance sheet.

The real price of a cross-border payment is not the rate. It is the rate multiplied by the time.

7. What I would tell an African CFO this week

  1. Stop holding idle sterling. Cash waiting for an invoice in a non-interest account is now a real loss.
  2. Measure your payment cycle in days, then in pounds. Every day saved in settlement is margin.
  3. Lock rates when markets are open. In a volatile month, the gap between a firm quote and an indicative one can be your profit.
  4. Watch 28 October and 5 November. The Budget, then the Bank of England’s next decision. A hike strengthens the case for converting early rather than late.
  5. Refinance before you have to. The window is open, but narrower than it looks.

The bond market has no ideology. It does not care about Westminster or Yaoundé, about speeches or slogans. It asks one question of everyone: what is your time worth?

For fifteen years, the answer was “almost nothing”, and the world built its payment systems around that illusion. In October 2026, London’s answer is 6%. Those who understand what that means will spend the next decade making time cheap again. The others will keep paying for it, three days at a time.

AI

Intelligence on Tap: Who Will Own the Meter?

Intelligence is no longer just a technology. It has become a matter of state, a matter of geopolitics, and very soon, a monthly bill.

Mohamed Ramadan
6 October 2026 · 5 min readAIUnited StatesAfrica

Key points

  • On 29 September, the leaders of the AI industry met at the White House and signed a voluntary accord to police themselves.
  • Tokens are to intelligence what kilowatt-hours are to electricity: the unit of a new utility.
  • Global debt is now above $365 trillion, with AI infrastructure among the forces behind the latest record.
  • The next decades will be decided by who produces intelligence, who finances it, and who sets its price.

Last Tuesday, a single room in Washington held more of the world’s future than most parliaments.

On 29 September, President Trump hosted the leaders of the AI industry at the White House: Anthropic’s Dario Amodei, Elon Musk, Mark Zuckerberg, Sundar Pichai, Jensen Huang, Jeff Bezos, OpenAI’s Greg Brockman and others. They left having signed a voluntary accord to police themselves. A few days earlier, many of the same people had sat at the state dinner for China’s President Xi.

Read those two scenes together and you see the century we have entered. Intelligence is no longer just a technology. It has become a matter of state, a matter of geopolitics, and very soon, a monthly bill.

AI is becoming the new electricity

A hundred years ago, a factory without electricity was not a slightly less efficient factory. It was a dead factory. Twenty years ago, a business without internet access was not old-fashioned. It was invisible.

AI is following the same path, only faster. Within a decade, I believe access to intelligence will be a utility, like power, water or broadband. Every household, every company and every government will pay a subscription for it. You will not ask whether your business uses AI, any more than you ask today whether it uses electricity. You will ask how much it consumes, at what price, and from whom.

The unit of this new economy is already here: the token. Tokens are to intelligence what kilowatt-hours are to electricity. Every email drafted, every contract reviewed, every credit analysed and every line of code written by a machine is measured, priced and billed in tokens.

The new divide: those who have tokens, and those who do not

Here is the uncomfortable part. Electricity was eventually distributed to almost everyone. Intelligence may not be, at least not equally.

In the coming decades, the advantage of a company, a city or a country will depend on how much intelligence it can afford to consume. A firm with a large token budget will analyse more, test more, serve more clients and move faster than a firm rationing every query. The token budget will sit next to payroll and rent on every income statement, and for many businesses, it will become the largest line.

Those who control the production of intelligence, the chips, the data centres and the energy that feeds them, will hold a position comparable to the oil majors of the twentieth century. That is why a lunch at the White House matters to an entrepreneur in Douala, Lagos or London.

The money behind the machine

This revolution is also a financial one. The data centres, power plants and chips behind AI require capital on a scale the world has rarely seen. The Institute of International Finance identified AI infrastructure, alongside emerging markets and defence spending, as one of the forces behind the latest record in global debt, now above $365 trillion.

We are financing a new industrial base, largely with borrowed money. As with railways and electricity before it, some of this investment will build lasting wealth, and some will end in painful corrections. The financiers who understand which is which will shape the next decades.

What happens to work

I do not believe AI will end work. I believe it will change what we are paid for.

Tasks that can be described can increasingly be delegated: drafting, summarising, calculating, translating, checking. What remains scarce, and therefore valuable, is what cannot be easily described: judgement, trust, relationships, accountability and the courage to decide. A machine can prepare ten financing structures in a minute. Choosing the right one, and convincing a bank and a client to sign it, remains deeply human.

Every professional will soon work with a team of AI assistants, paid for by subscription, the way we pay today for a phone and a laptop. The question for each of us is simple: will we manage that team, or be replaced by someone who does?

Even the builders want to slow down

What struck me most about the White House meeting was not who was there, but why. In recent weeks, Dario Amodei called on companies to “pace the frontier” of the most advanced models, and Sam Altman and Elon Musk agreed with calls for an industry-wide slowdown.

When the people building a technology ask for brakes, the rest of us should listen. Power on this scale, concentrated in a handful of companies and a few countries, raises questions that markets alone will not answer: who sets the rules, who audits the systems, and who decides what intelligence costs.

What it means for Africa

Africa cannot afford to be only a consumer of intelligence, paying for it in dollars and importing it like fuel. We have done this before with energy and paid the price.

But Africa also has a history of leapfrogging. We went straight to mobile phones without building landlines, and straight to mobile money without building bank branches in every village. The same can happen with AI, if we invest in energy, data centres, skills and the financing that makes them possible.

This is where finance becomes strategy. The countries and companies that secure capital for this infrastructure today will own a share of the meter tomorrow. The others will simply pay the bill.

Who will own the meter?

Every great utility of the past century created two kinds of people: those who owned the network, and those who paid for access. AI will do the same, at a speed and scale we have never experienced.

The next decades will not be decided by who uses AI. Everyone will. They will be decided by who produces it, who finances it, and who sets the price of a thought.

I know which side I want my companies, my clients and my continent to be on.

  • Institute of International Finance, Global Debt Monitor, 23 September 2026

Note · Economics

“In the long run we are all dead.”

John Maynard Keynes, A Tract on Monetary Reform, 1923

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Keynes is often quoted as if he were dismissing the future. He was doing the opposite. The sentence attacks economists who promise that markets will "eventually" correct, while people lose jobs, homes and savings in the meantime. Its lesson for policy is that timing is not a detail. A recession that "corrects itself" in seven years has already destroyed a decade of careers. For a finance director, the same logic applies: a business that will be fine "in the long run" can still run out of cash next quarter. Liquidity is the bridge between today and the long run, and the bridge has to hold.

“The difficulty lies not so much in developing new ideas as in escaping from old ones.”

John Maynard Keynes, The General Theory, 1936

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

This is the most honest sentence in economics. Our models, habits and incentives are built around assumptions that once worked. When the world changes, the hardest part is not imagining a new framework but abandoning the comfortable one. The fifteen years of near-zero rates are a perfect example: a whole generation of investors, treasurers and policymakers learned to treat money as free. Unlearning that is painful, and those who resist it pay the bill in higher funding costs and broken business models. Intellectual humility is not modesty; it is a competitive advantage.

Note · Economics

“Inflation is always and everywhere a monetary phenomenon.”

Milton Friedman, 1970

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Friedman's line is a starting point, not the whole story. Over long periods, sustained inflation does require too much money chasing too few goods. But 2022 and the energy shocks since have shown that supply disruptions, wars and energy prices can drive inflation in the short run, and that central banks then face a choice: accommodate the shock or fight its spread into wages and expectations. The enduring truth in Friedman's sentence is accountability. Whatever the trigger, it is monetary policy that decides whether a price shock becomes a permanent inflation problem.

“Nothing is so permanent as a temporary government programme.”

Milton Friedman

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Every government announces temporary measures in a crisis: subsidies, tax reliefs, emergency spending. Many quietly become permanent because beneficiaries organise to defend them and politicians fear the cost of withdrawal. That is why a temporary bank surcharge that ends after fifteen months, or a fuel duty cut extended "until July", deserves scrutiny. Fiscal credibility depends on whether "temporary" really means temporary. Bond markets have learned to price the difference between the announcement and the likely reality.

“There is no such thing as a free lunch.”

Title of a book by Milton Friedman, 1975

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

The phrase is older than Friedman, but he made it a principle. Every choice has an opportunity cost, even when the price is hidden. Near-zero interest rates looked like a free lunch for a decade; the bill arrived as inflation, asset bubbles and a painful repricing of debt. The same applies to "free" digital services paid for with data, or to government spending financed by borrowing that future taxpayers repay. The discipline of economics is to ask, every time: who pays, when, and how?

Note · Economics

“It is not from the benevolence of the butcher, the brewer, or the baker that we expect our dinner, but from their regard to their own interest.”

Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Smith's insight is that markets coordinate millions of self-interested decisions into outcomes that serve others, without anyone planning them. It remains the strongest argument for competition. But Smith also wrote The Theory of Moral Sentiments, and warned against merchants conspiring against the public. Self-interest works for society only inside rules: property rights, contracts, competition law and trust. Where those institutions are weak, as in many emerging markets, self-interest can produce monopoly and capture instead of prosperity.

Note · Economics

“Economics is a study of mankind in the ordinary business of life.”

Alfred Marshall, Principles of Economics, 1890

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Marshall's definition is a reminder that economics is about people, not equations. Rates, yields and spreads matter because they shape rent, wages, food prices and the decision to start a business. When analysis loses sight of the ordinary business of life, it becomes technically impressive and practically useless. My test for any piece I write is simple: could I explain to a shopkeeper in Douala or a nurse in Manchester why this number matters to them?

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Krugman's line explains why some countries grow rich and others stall. Over decades, living standards depend on how much each hour of work produces. Britain's productivity slowdown since 2008 is, in my view, the single most important economic story behind its fiscal difficulties: without productivity growth, every promise on public services must be paid for with higher taxes or more debt. For Africa, the same principle explains why investment in infrastructure, energy and skills matters more than any short-term stimulus.

Note · Economics

“The curious task of economics is to demonstrate to men how little they really know about what they imagine they can design.”

Friedrich Hayek, The Fatal Conceit, 1988

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Hayek warns against the planner's pride: the belief that a central authority can know enough to design an economy. Prices aggregate information that no single mind possesses. That warning applies to companies as much as governments. A five-year plan built on precise forecasts of demand, prices and rates is almost certainly wrong. The better approach is to build organisations that learn quickly, keep options open and respond to signals rather than defend the plan.

Note · Economics

“Development can be seen as a process of expanding the real freedoms that people enjoy.”

Amartya Sen, Development as Freedom, 1999

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Sen changed how we measure progress. GDP growth matters, but development is ultimately about what people are able to do and to be: to be educated, healthy, to participate politically, to choose their work. This perspective is vital for Africa. Growth that enriches a few while leaving schools, clinics and roads behind is not development. The best economic policies expand capabilities: they make it possible for people to use their talent.

Note · Economics

“If something cannot go on forever, it will stop.”

Herbert Stein, economist (Stein’s Law)

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Stein's Law sounds obvious, which is why it is so often ignored. Current account deficits, rising debt ratios, asset prices growing faster than incomes, companies borrowing to pay dividends: all can continue for a surprisingly long time, and then stop abruptly. The value of the law is not in predicting when, but in forcing us to identify which trends are unsustainable and to prepare for their end before the market forces the adjustment.

Note · Economics

“Stability is destabilizing.”

Hyman Minsky

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Minsky's insight is that long periods of calm encourage risk-taking. When nothing has gone wrong for years, lenders relax standards, borrowers take more leverage and investors treat volatility as a thing of the past. The system becomes fragile precisely because it looks safe. The 2008 crisis was a Minsky moment, and so, on a smaller scale, are many sudden reversals in emerging-market debt. Risk management means being most cautious when everyone else feels most comfortable.

Note · Economics

“The first lesson of economics is scarcity: there is never enough of anything to fully satisfy all those who want it. The first lesson of politics is to disregard the first lesson of economics.”

Thomas Sowell

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Sowell captures the permanent tension between economics and politics. Resources are limited, so every choice means giving up something else. Politics rewards promises that ignore this. Budgets are where the two collide: every new commitment must be financed by taxes, borrowing or cuts elsewhere. The most credible finance ministers are those who state the trade-offs openly. Markets punish governments that pretend the first lesson does not apply to them.

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Solow wrote this in 1987. The productivity gains from computers did eventually appear, in the late 1990s, after companies reorganised around the technology. The same question now hangs over artificial intelligence. Investment is enormous; measurable productivity gains are still modest. History suggests the gains come, but only when organisations redesign how work is done, not when they simply add new tools to old processes. The lag matters for investors who are financing the build-out today.

Note · Economics

“Inflation is taxation without legislation.”

Milton Friedman

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Inflation transfers wealth from savers and wage earners to debtors, including governments, without any vote. It reduces the real value of public debt while eroding the purchasing power of fixed incomes. That is why central bank independence matters: it removes the temptation to inflate away debts. It is also why inflation hurts the poor most, since they hold cash and have the least power to renegotiate wages or prices.

“A cynic is a man who knows the price of everything and the value of nothing.”

Oscar Wilde, Lady Windermere’s Fan, 1892

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Wilde was writing about people, but the line describes a common failure in finance. Markets are very good at pricing what is traded and measurable, and poor at valuing what is not: trust, institutions, the environment, a company's culture. Good investors know that price and value can diverge for long periods. The opportunity lies in that gap, and so does the risk.

Note · Economics

“Debt is the slavery of the free.”

Publilius Syrus, 1st century BC

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Publilius Syrus wrote two thousand years ago, but the warning fits every era of cheap credit. Debt is a powerful tool: it finances houses, factories and infrastructure. But it also binds future income to past decisions. A country or a company that borrows heavily loses freedom of action exactly when it needs it most, in a crisis. The question is never whether to borrow, but how much flexibility the debt leaves.

“Money is a terrible master but an excellent servant.”

P. T. Barnum

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Barnum's line applies to companies as well as individuals. Used well, money finances growth, absorbs shocks and creates options. When the pursuit of short-term financial targets drives every decision, it becomes a master: companies cut investment to meet quarterly numbers, borrow to fund buybacks and lose sight of their customers. A good finance function keeps money in its place: serving the strategy, not replacing it.

Note · Finance

“Rule No. 1: Never lose money. Rule No. 2: Never forget rule No. 1.”

Warren Buffett

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Buffett's rule is a statement about the mathematics of losses. A 50% loss requires a 100% gain to recover. Avoiding large losses matters more than capturing every gain. In practice, it means understanding what you own, refusing leverage that can force a sale at the worst time, and treating the downside as seriously as the upside. Preservation of capital is the first job of any treasurer.

1 min read

Why it matters

When liquidity is abundant, weak business models and excessive leverage are hidden. When rates rise and credit tightens, they are exposed. That is what is happening in 2026 as the cost of money returns: companies and countries that relied on cheap refinancing are being tested. The time to check whether you are swimming naked is before the tide goes out.

Note · Finance

“In the short run, the market is a voting machine but in the long run, it is a weighing machine.”

Benjamin Graham, as quoted by Warren Buffett

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Graham's distinction explains why prices can move far from value. In the short run, prices reflect popularity, fear and momentum. Over the long run, they reflect earnings and cash flows. Patient investors exploit the gap between the two. Impatient ones are its victims. Record IPO volumes in 2026 are, in part, a voting-machine phenomenon: the real test comes when the weighing machine takes over.

Note · Finance

“The investor’s chief problem, and even his worst enemy, is likely to be himself.”

Benjamin Graham, The Intelligent Investor, 1949

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Graham understood that the greatest danger to returns is behaviour, not information. Fear and greed lead investors to buy high and sell low. Overconfidence leads to concentration and leverage. The best defence is a process: written rules, diversification, regular rebalancing and a refusal to make major decisions in moments of panic or euphoria.

“The essence of investment management is the management of risks, not the management of returns.”

Benjamin Graham

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Returns are uncertain; risks can be managed. A disciplined investor decides first how much can be lost, then how much can be gained. This principle applies equally to corporate treasury, where the priority is liquidity and capital preservation, not maximising yield on cash. Many treasury disasters began with the search for a few extra basis points.

Sir John Templeton

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Templeton's description of the market cycle is a map for investors. At the bottom, everyone is pessimistic and prices are low. At the top, everyone is euphoric and prices are high. Recognising the stage of the cycle is more useful than predicting the next quarter. Signs of euphoria include record issuance, rising leverage and the belief that prices can only go up.

Note · Finance

“Within our mandate, the ECB is ready to do whatever it takes to preserve the euro. And believe me, it will be enough.”

Mario Draghi, London, 26 July 2012

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Draghi's three words saved the euro without the ECB spending a single euro at the time. Credibility, not money, did the work: markets believed the central bank would act, so they stopped betting against weaker members. The lesson for policymakers everywhere is that a credible commitment can be more powerful than intervention itself. The lesson for markets is never to fight a central bank that means what it says.

Emanuel's line is often quoted cynically, but it describes something real: crises create the political will for reforms that would be impossible in calm times. Banking regulation after 2008, digital payments after the pandemic, energy policy after supply shocks. The danger is that crises also produce rushed decisions. The best reforms are prepared in advance, so they are ready when the window opens.

1 min read

Why it matters

Bezos's warning to incumbents is a law of competition: high margins attract competitors. Businesses that rely on opaque pricing or customer inertia are vulnerable to anyone who offers more for less. Cross-border payments are a clear example: high fees and slow transfers have created space for new providers. In the long run, excess margins are temporary unless they are protected by real advantages.

“Management is doing things right; leadership is doing the right things.”

Peter Drucker

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Drucker's distinction is essential for anyone who leads. Management is about efficiency: processes, budgets, execution. Leadership is about direction: choosing what to do and what not to do. A company can be perfectly managed and still fail if it is heading the wrong way. The finance function often focuses on doing things right. Its greatest value comes when it also helps the organisation decide what the right things are.

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

Turing's closing sentence is a model of humility about technology. He did not claim to know where machine intelligence would lead, only that there was much work to do. Why it matters

This is the core idea of my analysis Intelligence on Tap. Every task performed by an AI system is measured and billed in tokens, just as electricity is billed in kilowatt-hours. The companies and countries that can afford abundant intelligence will move faster than those that must ration it.

Why it matters

Ubuntu expresses a view of humanity as interconnected. It has practical implications for economics and leadership: trust, community and reciprocity are forms of capital. Informal savings groups, family remittances and community lending across Africa are expressions of this philosophy. Formal finance works best when it builds on these networks rather than ignoring them.

For Africa's economic development, the long road together, through regional markets and shared infrastructure, is the one that leads furthest.

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

From The Price of Time. African economies pay higher interest on debt and higher fees on remittances. Sending $200 to sub-Saharan Africa costs 8.46% on average, against 6.36% worldwide. In a world of higher rates, slow and expensive payments are a hidden tax. Reducing that cost is one of the most direct ways to keep more value on the continent.

Mohamed Ramadan, The Price of Time, 2026

Why it matters

The central formula of The Price of Time. A payment's true cost includes the time money spends in transit, multiplied by the cost of money. When rates were near zero, delay was almost free. At today's rates, it is a real expense. Faster settlement is now a source of margin.

Note · Finance

“The bond market has no ideology. … It asks one question of everyone: what is your time worth?”

Mohamed Ramadan, The Price of Time, 2026

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

The closing idea of The Price of Time. Bond investors do not care about speeches or slogans. They ask whether a borrower can repay, on time, in a currency that holds its value. Every government, from Westminster to Yaoundé, faces the same test. Credibility is earned through consistent policy, not announcements.

Note · Leadership

“A machine can prepare ten financing structures in a minute. Choosing the right one, and convincing a bank and a client to sign it, remains deeply human.”

Mohamed Ramadan, Intelligence on Tap, 2026

Commentary by Mohamed Ramadan
1 min read

Why it matters

From Intelligence on Tap. AI will automate much of the preparation work in finance: models, analyses, drafts. What remains human is judgement, negotiation and trust: choosing the right structure and convincing others to commit to it. That is where professionals will add value in the decade ahead.
